title: Book 6 — Erato, Chapter 109
paragraphs: The opinions of the Athenian generals were divided. One side argued that they should not fight a battle, since they were too few to engage the Median army; the other side, among them Miltiades, argued that they should. The worse opinion was on the point of prevailing. But since the man chosen by lot as polemarch of Athens had a vote in addition to the ten generals (for in those days the Athenians gave the polemarch an equal vote with the generals), and the polemarch at that time was Callimachus of the deme of Aphidnae, Miltiades came to him and said: “Callimachus, it rests with you now either to bring Athens into slavery, or to leave her free and so bequeath to all future generations a memorial even greater than Harmodius and Aristogiton left. For at this moment the Athenians face a greater danger than any they have faced since they became a people. If they submit to the Medes, it is already decided what they shall suffer, being handed over to Hippias; but if this city prevails, she may become the foremost of all the cities of Greece. How that may happen, and why the decision has fallen to you of all men, I shall now explain. Of us ten generals, the opinions are divided, some urging battle, some opposing it. If we do not fight, I expect some great spirit of discord will fall upon the Athenians and so shake them that they will go over to the Medes. But if we fight a battle before any rot can set in among the people, then — if the gods grant us a fair field — we can win. All of this now lies with you and depends on you. If you join my side, your country is free and your native city will be the first among the cities of Greece. If you choose the side of those who oppose battle, you will have the opposite of all the goods I have described.”
